metadata.title: How a Gas Price Shock Spreads to Other Prices
metadata.data_notes: Chart starts in 2003 because the bond-market inflation expectation series (T5YIFR) begins then.

events.label: Financial crisis: gas falls to $1.75, inflation near 0%
Core inflation peaks at 6.6%, 3 months after gas

explanation.summary: When gas prices jump at the pump, how fast does the rest of your budget follow? The three cards show a chain: the gas price compared with a year ago, overall inflation (all prices), and "everyday" prices (core inflation: everything except food and energy). The stripes below show every month since 2004: red is higher than normal, blue is lower. Gas and overall inflation move together in the same month. Everyday prices follow more slowly and only when the shock lasts: in 2022 they peaked three months after gas did.
explanation.methodology: Monthly average retail price of regular gasoline from the Energy Information Administration (EIA). Overall and core consumer price inflation are year-over-year changes in the BLS Consumer Price Index (CPI-U). Expected future inflation is the 5-year, 5-year-forward rate from FRED (T5YIFR), averaged by month. The chart starts in 2003, the first year of that bond-market series.

key_findings.title: July 2008: $4.11 Gas, 5.6% Inflation
key_findings.description: Oil prices hit a record and a gallon of regular averaged $4.11. Overall inflation rose to 5.6%. Core inflation barely moved, staying near 2.5%.
key_findings.significance: A gas spike alone lifts the headline number fast but does not spread to everything else when it is short.

key_findings.title: December 2008: The Crash
key_findings.description: In five months gas fell to $1.75 and overall inflation dropped to almost zero. Bond traders' expected future inflation collapsed to 0.73%, the lowest on the chart.
key_findings.significance: Markets feared falling prices (deflation), not rising ones, at the depth of the financial crisis.

key_findings.title: June 2022: $5.03 Gas, 9.1% Inflation
key_findings.description: Gas averaged $5.03, the highest on record, and overall inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. This time core inflation kept climbing and peaked at 6.6% in September 2022, three months after gas.
key_findings.significance: When high energy costs last long enough, they leak into rents, services and everyday goods.
